extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners, and patent examiners handling reissue applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes an "error" allowing filing of a reissue application under 35 U.S.C. 251, with examples, limits, and alternatives (e.g., certificate of correction) and procedural pointers (e.g., petition types and fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for filing a reissue application
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue application is filed to correct an error in the patent, where, as a result of the error, the patent is deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid. An error in the patent arises out of an error in conduct which was made in the preparation and/or prosecution of the application which became the patent. There must be at least one error in the patent to provide grounds for reissue of the patent. If there is no error in the patent, the patent will not be reissued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the fundamental threshold: an identifiable error rooted in preparation/prosecution that causes the patent to be wholly or partly inoperative or invalid. Procedural cross-references include 35 U.S.C. 251 and MPEP sections (e.g., §1481 for certificates of correction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory standard under 35 U.S.C. 251
rubrics_metrics.description: The error upon which reissue is based must be one which causes the patent to be 'deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective specification or drawing, or by reason of the patentee claiming more or less than he had a right to claim in the patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-substantive corrections — spelling, grammar, typographical, editorial or clerical errors — that do not cause the patent to be deemed wholly or partly inoperative or invalid under 35 U.S.C. 251 do not provide a basis for reissue; such corrections may be made via a certificate of correction (see MPEP §1481). Non-substantive corrections may be included in a reissue only where a qualifying 35 U.S.C. 251 error is already present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common bases for filing a reissue application
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common bases for filing a reissue application are: (A) the claims are too narrow or too broad; (B) the disclosure contains inaccuracies; (C) applicant failed to or incorrectly claimed foreign priority; and (D) applicant failed to make reference to or incorrectly made reference to prior copending applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four categories summarize frequent factual/legal errors giving rise to reissue. Each has its own sub-rules and potential alternatives (e.g., certificates of correction or petitions) discussed elsewhere in the section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error based on scope of claims (adding narrower claims / claiming less or more than entitled)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue error may be directed solely to the failure to previously present narrower claims, which are being added by reissue. The omission of a narrower claim from a patent can render a patent partly inoperative by failing to protect the disclosed invention to the full extent allowed by law. This permits submission of additional claims that are narrower in scope than the preexisting patent claims, without any narrowing of the preexisting patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and limits: a reissue applicant can retain broad independent claims while adding new dependent (narrower) claims. However, an applicant's failure to timely file a divisional application covering non-elected inventions following a restriction requirement is NOT considered an error correctable by reissue (see MPEP §1412.01). Case law: In re Tanaka (omission of narrower claim), In re Wilder (attorney's failure to appreciate scope can be correctable), and Medrad (error may be 'any error that causes a patentee to claim more or less than he had a right to claim').

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship error (misjoinder/correction of inventors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction of misjoinder of inventors in reissues has been held to be a ground for reissue. If the only change being made in the patent is correction of the inventorship, this can be accomplished by filing a request for a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 256 and 37 CFR 1.324.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A certificate of correction will be issued if all parties are in agreement and the inventorship issue is not contested (see MPEP §§1412.04 and 1481). Alternatively, an applicant may choose to file a reissue application to correct inventorship because misjoinder is an error correctable under 35 U.S.C. 251.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error related to foreign priority (failure to file certified copy / perfect priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue was granted where the only ground urged was failure to file a certified copy of the original foreign application to obtain the right of foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) before the patent was granted. Reissue is also available to correct the 'error' in failing to take steps to obtain the right of foreign priority before grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting or perfecting a foreign priority claim in a reissue, the applicant must consider the 37 CFR 1.55 rules: file the appropriate petition under 37 CFR 1.55(f) or (g) (including a showing of good and sufficient cause) or under 1.55(e) for an unintentionally delayed priority claim. In some situations a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323, accompanied by an appropriate 1.55 petition, may be the preferable route. The petition requirements are the same whether using reissue or certificate of correction, and certain combinations (e.g., submitting the certified copy with a 1.55(e) petition) eliminate the need for other petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error in benefit claim to domestic application (unintentionally delayed benefit claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to law (PLTIA) and 37 CFR 1.78(c) permit acceptance of unintentionally delayed benefit claims to a provisional application after the patent was granted, provided certain petition requirements are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements for a petition under 37 CFR 1.78(c) include: (1) the reference required by 35 U.S.C. 119(e) and 37 CFR 1.78(a)(3) to the prior-filed provisional application (unless previously submitted); (2) the petition fee as set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m); and (3) a statement that the entire delay between the due date and filing was unintentional. The Director may require additional information. Similar petitioning procedures apply for unintentionally delayed benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c)/386(c) via 37 CFR 1.78(e). For some priority/benefit corrections, a certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323 accompanied by a grantable 1.55 petition may be appropriate (see MPEP §§211.04, 214, 216.01). Also: a patentee cannot obtain the 35 U.S.C. 121 safe harbor against nonstatutory double patenting by deleting new matter from a CIP via reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error in drawings (substantive vs non-substantive drawing corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue may be based on a drawing correction that is substantive in nature, because such a correction qualifies as correcting an error under 35 U.S.C. 251 that may properly be deemed to render the patent wholly or partly inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-substantive drawing changes — e.g., a reference numeral correction or addition, the addition of shading, or the addition of an additional figure merely to clarify the disclosure — cannot serve as the basis for a reissue application. However, non-substantive drawing changes may be included in a reissue application that corrects at least one substantive error under 35 U.S.C. 251.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error in filing terminal disclaimer is generally not a reissue ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a terminal disclaimer to obviate a double patenting rejection over a prior patent, when the prior patent and the patent sought to be reissued were never commonly owned, was held not to be an error within the meaning of the reissue statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Dinsmore) indicates that applicants attempting to revise a choice they made (e.g., filing a terminal disclaimer where the requisite ownership relationship did not exist or was not mistakenly believed) are not obtaining a remedy via reissue; they must show a mistaken belief, not just a desire to change a prior decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use certificate of correction versus reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain corrections (spelling, grammar, typographical, editorial, clerical) that do not cause the patent to be wholly or partly inoperative do not provide a basis for reissue and instead may be made via a certificate of correction (35 U.S.C. 255/256; 37 CFR 1.323/1.324).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance throughout the section directs patentees to consider a certificate of correction when appropriate (e.g., for non-substantive errors or where a priority claim was timely filed but the certified copy requirement was not satisfied). Where a certificate of correction is used to add or perfect a priority/benefit claim, the same petition requirements (37 CFR 1.55 or 1.78) generally apply as when filing reissue. See MPEP §§1481, 216.01, 214, 211.04 for details.
